fatal_errors: The material is incorrectly treated as a single-phase random solid solution, whereas the target is an as-cast FCC+B2 eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy.
The governing intervention is incorrectly assigned to dynamic high-strain-rate loading rather than controlled intermediate-temperature aging.
The hypothesis omits the non-monotonic ductile-brittle-ductile transition, including maximum embrittlement near 600°C and recovery near 750°C.
It omits the coupled role of enhanced L12 ordering and jagged FCC/B2 phase-boundary tips in dislocation pile-up, stress concentration, and crack initiation.
The proposed test confounds prior loading history with mechanical response instead of aging specimens separately and then testing all conditions under identical loading.
The cited evidence does not establish mechanically induced local ordering or resulting brittle fracture in this alloy and service regime.
explanation: The generated hypothesis captures only a broad fragment of the target mechanism: chemical ordering can increase barriers to dislocation motion and reduce plasticity. It does not reconstruct the specific alloy, its initial dual-phase microstructure, the 550–750°C aging window, L12 ordering near Ni3Al stoichiometry, jagged B2/FCC boundaries, or ductile transition zones responsible for recovery at higher aging temperature. Its predicted response is monotonic embrittlement under dynamic loading rather than the observed ductile-brittle-ductile aging response. The experiment is nominally falsifiable and includes useful TEM and mechanical measurements, but its controls are confounded and it does not target dislocation pile-ups and crack initiation at jagged phase-boundary tips or exclude grain-boundary impurity segregation. E3 supports ordering-related dislocation resistance in HEAs generally, while E1 concerns ceramics and E2 is a broad review; none validates the proposed strain-induced ordering and brittle-fracture pathway.
